source_text: Iure igitur hoc genere dicitur abundasse delictum, quod et ante legem et post legem uniuscuiusque committebat voluntas; sed ante legem peccatrix, post legem autem etiam praevaricatrix. Tunc ergo crescit et abundat aliquid, cum in genere suo colligit incrementa, sicut peccato liberae voluntatis post Moysen cumulus transgressionis accessit; de eodem enim genere fuit, licet in tempore diverso, id est de mala voluntate, quae et ante legem et post legem non coactu insuperabili, sed studio vituperabili deliquit. Quae cum ita sint, tibi nihil potest de apostolicis convenire verbis; neque enim subintroeunte lege peccatum traducis aut copiosius factum docetur aut grandius; nec peccatis voluntatis illud abundare iure dicitur, quod ad nascentium voluntatem nequaquam attinere monstratur. Non ergo abundavit post legem, quod lex nec prohibere potuit nec punire. Ubi autem abundavit peccatum, superabundavit gratia, ut sicut regnavit peccatum in mortem, ita gratia regnet per iustitiam in vitam aeternam [n369] .
pass_a_gloss: Rightly therefore in this kind the offense is said to have abounded, which both before the law and after the law the will of each one was committing; but before the law sinful, but after the law also transgressing. Then therefore something grows and abounds, when it collects increments in its own kind, as after Moses a heap of transgression acceded to a sin of free will; for it was of the same kind, although in a diverse time, that is of an evil will, which both before the law and after the law offended not by an insuperable compulsion, but by a vituperable pursuit. Which things being so, nothing of the apostolic words can fit you; for neither with the law entering under is the sin of the tradux taught as having been made more copious or greater; nor is that rightly said to abound to sins of will, which is shown in no way to belong to the will of those being born. It therefore did not abound after the law, which the law could neither prohibit nor punish. But where sin abounded, grace superabounded, so that as sin reigned unto death, so grace may reign through justice unto eternal life.

lemmas.lexica: LS praevaricatio; Blaise Adam's transgression as example
LS delictum; Blaise Rom 5 delictum vs donum
LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: In this sense, then, the offense is rightly said to have abounded: each person’s will committed it both before and after the law, but before the law the will was sinful, while after the law it was also transgressive. Something grows and abounds when it gains increase within its own kind, just as after Moses the additional weight of transgression was added to the sin of free will. For it belonged to the same kind, though at a different time: an evil will which sinned both before and after the law, not through irresistible compulsion, but through blameworthy effort. Since this is so, nothing in the apostle’s words can fit your position. The coming of the law is not shown to have made inherited sin more abundant or greater. Nor can something plainly unrelated to newborn children’s will rightly be said to abound through sins of will. Therefore what the law could neither prohibit nor punish did not abound after the law. ‘But where sin abounded, grace abounded beyond it, so that, just as sin reigned into death, grace might reign through righteousness into eternal life’ (Romans 5:20–21).
